doc.title: Jon-Erik Kellso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Calling tunes on the stand and the trumpeter's pressure
summary: At jazz parties musicians may meet cold; the trumpeter is expected to know and lead the melody.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: And how did you go about — was there a method to trying to memorize and learn these tunes? Because I’m always interested in how all these people fly in from different parts of the country, and this promoter, hopefully puts them together in workable ensembles, and then you get up there and the designated leader says, okay, here’s the tunes, let’s go.

Yeah. Sometimes you talk it over beforehand, sometimes you don’t. Sometimes you’re just on the stand and you’d better to know the song they call or else you’re going to be embarrassed or you’re going to be scuffling a little bit. And for the trumpet player it’s a little bit more pressure than the other guys in the band, because the trumpet player is generally expected to play the melody, at least so they can recognize it. And so I mean if you’re the clarinet player in the front line, playing sort of ensemble, free-wheeling kind of playing, if you’ve got good ears you can hear the chord changes even if you’ve never heard the song before, you can generally, you’ve got the first chorus to listen to the rhythm section and the trumpet player and sort of fill in. And you can get away with something. I mean not to put down any of the other members of the band, but it is a little bit of an extra pressure. You have to know the songs you know.
